title: Die Geschichte vom Suppen-Kaspar
source: Heinrich Hoffmann, Der Struwwelpeter, Rütten & Loening, Frankfurt am Main, 564. Auflage — the canonical later text in modernized spelling (via Project Gutenberg #24571). Fresh Lectorium translation from the German.
about: A story told as a calendar: on the first day Kaspar is round and rosy and eats his soup nicely at table, and then he refuses — and the verse simply counts off the days while he thins to a thread. Soup in a 19th-century household was not a side dish but the fixed opening course of the midday meal, so refusing it means refusing to eat at all. The refrain never changes; only the boy does, and Hoffmann draws no moral at the end — the last word is »tot«.

sentences.t:
Der Kaspar, der war kerngesund,
ein dicker Bub und kugelrund.
sentences.l:
The Kaspar, he was core-healthy,
a fat boy and ball-round.
sentences.i:
Kaspar was as sound as could be,
a fat boy, round as a ball.
sentences.n: »kerngesund« is literally ‘core-healthy’ — sound right through, from »Kern« (kernel, core); »kugelrund« is ‘ball-round,’ from »Kugel« (ball). Both are still everyday German. The name is picked up again by »der«: »Der Kaspar, der war …« — ‘Kaspar, he was …’, the same spoken shape as »Der Friederich, der Friederich«. »Bub« is the clipped »Bube« (boy) once more.

sentences.t:
Er hatte Backen rot und frisch;
die Suppe aß er hübsch bei Tisch.
sentences.l:
He had cheeks red and fresh;
the soup ate he nicely at table.
sentences.i:
His cheeks were red and fresh;
he ate his soup up nicely at table.
sentences.n: »Backen« are the cheeks — the plump, physical word (»Wangen« is the genteel one). »hübsch« is adverbial again: ‘nicely, properly,’ not ‘pretty.’ »bei Tisch«, with no article, is the fixed phrase for ‘at table, at meals.’ Adjectives set after their noun (»Backen rot und frisch«) are a verse liberty; prose would say »rote, frische Backen«.

sentences.t: Doch einmal fing er an zu schrein:
sentences.l: But once began he on to scream:
sentences.i: But one day he started shouting:
sentences.n: »anfangen« (‘to begin’) is separable, and its »an« is stranded before the infinitive: »fing er an zu schrein«. »einmal« here is ‘one day, on one occasion.’ »schrein« is »schreien« clipped for the rhyme; the verb covers shouting as much as screaming.

sentences.t:
»Ich esse keine Suppe! nein!
Ich esse meine Suppe nicht!
Nein, meine Suppe eß ich nicht!«
sentences.l:
“I eat no soup! no!
I eat my soup not!
No, my soup eat I not!”
sentences.i:
“I’m not eating any soup! No!
I will not eat my soup!
No, my soup I will not eat!”
sentences.n: One refusal three times over, tightening each time: »keine Suppe« negates the soup itself, »nicht« at the end negates the whole sentence, and the last line throws »meine Suppe« to the front for emphasis, which pushes the verb into second place (»eß ich«). German uses the plain present where English reaches for ‘will’ — this is refusal, not description. »eß« is »esse« with the -e clipped, in the pre-reform spelling (today »ess«).

sentences.t:
Am nächsten Tag, – ja sieh nur her!
da war er schon viel magerer.
sentences.l:
On the next day, – yes look only this-way!
there was he already much thinner.
sentences.i:
The next day — yes, just look! —
he was already much thinner.
sentences.n: »sieh nur her!« — »hersehen« is separable (‘to look this way’), and »nur« after an imperative is ‘just,’ as in the Friederich’s »höre nur«. The poem is pointing at its own picture. »mager« is ‘lean, thin’; »magerer« the comparative. The »da« that opens the second line is the loose narrative ‘there, then’ — English usually leaves it out.

sentences.t: Da fing er wieder an zu schrein:
sentences.l: There began he again on to scream:
sentences.n: Only the frame-line changes from day to day (»Doch einmal« → »Da … wieder« → »gleich … wieder«); the words that follow never do.

sentences.t:
»Ich esse keine Suppe! nein!
Ich esse meine Suppe nicht!
Nein, meine Suppe eß ich nicht!«
sentences.l:
“I eat no soup! no!
I eat my soup not!
No, my soup eat I not!”
sentences.i:
“I’m not eating any soup! No!
I will not eat my soup!
No, my soup I will not eat!”

sentences.t:
Am dritten Tag, o weh und ach!
wie ist der Kaspar dünn und schwach!
sentences.l:
On the third day, o woe and alas!
how is the Kaspar thin and weak!
sentences.i:
On the third day — oh, woe and alas! —
how thin and weak Kaspar is!
sentences.n: »o weh und ach« is a set cry of dismay, two old lament-words yoked together. The tense steps into the present (»wie ist«): the story moves up close, as the Daumenlutscher does at its end. In a German »wie …!« exclamation the verb stands second — »wie ist der Kaspar dünn« where English says ‘how thin Kaspar is.’

sentences.t:
Doch als die Suppe kam herein,
gleich fing er wieder an zu schrein:
sentences.l:
But when the soup came in,
at-once began he again on to scream:
sentences.i:
But when the soup came in,
at once he started shouting again:
sentences.n: »hereinkommen« (‘to come in’) is separable: »kam … herein«. »als« is the ‘when’ of one particular past occasion (»wenn« would mean ‘whenever’). »gleich« = ‘right away.’ Note that the soup comes in by itself, grammatically — no one carries it; German is content to let the dish do the arriving.

sentences.t:
»Ich esse keine Suppe! nein!
Ich esse meine Suppe nicht!
Nein, meine Suppe eß ich nicht!«
sentences.l:
“I eat no soup! no!
I eat my soup not!
No, my soup eat I not!”
sentences.i:
“I’m not eating any soup! No!
I will not eat my soup!
No, my soup I will not eat!”

sentences.t:
Am vierten Tage endlich gar
der Kaspar wie ein Fädchen war.
sentences.l:
On the fourth day finally even
the Kaspar like a little-thread was.
sentences.i:
On the fourth day, at last of all,
Kaspar was like a little thread.
sentences.n: »Fädchen« is »Faden« (thread) with the diminutive -chen: ‘a little thread.’ »gar« is the climax word again — ‘even, no less.’ »am vierten Tage« keeps the old dative -e that the earlier stanzas drop; both forms were current, and the meter chooses. Prose order would be »der Kaspar war endlich gar wie ein Fädchen«.

sentences.t:
Er wog vielleicht ein halbes Lot –
und war am fünften Tage tot.
sentences.l:
He weighed perhaps a half Lot –
and was on the fifth day dead.
sentences.i:
He weighed perhaps half a Lot —
and on the fifth day he was dead.
sentences.n: A »Lot« was a small pre-metric weight, roughly half an ounce (about 14–17 grams, varying from state to state) — so half a Lot is nothing at all. »wog« is the past of »wiegen« (to weigh). The ending is delivered flat, in the same breath as the weighing: no rescue, no lesson, and »tot« as the last word.
